I could not derive this from first principles, and I am recalling the result from memory rather than verifying it, so treat it with some caution.

- **Width is not 1.** $\mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N}$ is non-commutative: for example, $f(n)=n+1$ and $g(n)=2n$ satisfy $f\circ g\neq g\circ f$. So a single commutative submonoid cannot equal the whole monoid.
- **Width 2 is, to my recollection, attainable.** I recall a result on decompositions of full transformation monoids into products of commutative submonoids, stating that $\mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N}$ (the full transformation monoid on a countably infinite set) is the product of two commutative submonoids. I did not reconstruct the explicit factorization, so this rests on that recollection.

ANSWER: 2
